name: Beef steak
description: A 300 g steak needs about 4,600 liters, enough for 60 showers. Most of it goes into the cattle's feed.

source.title: Mekonnen & Hoekstra (2012), A global assessment of the water footprint of farm animal products, Ecosystems 15:401

name: Beef burger
description: One 150 g burger with its bun needs about 2,400 liters, mostly for the cow's years of grain and grass.

source.title: Water Footprint Network, Product Gallery

name: Sheet of paper
description: A single A4 sheet needs 2 to 13 liters, mostly for growing the trees.

source.title: Van Oel & Hoekstra (2012), Towards quantification of the water footprint of paper, Water Resources Management 26:733
source.basis: 80 g/m2 A4 sheet; study range 2-13 L

name: Smartphone
description: A smartphone needs about 12,760 liters, across mining, manufacturing and assembly.

source.title: Friends of the Earth (2015), Mind Your Step: the land and water footprints of everyday products

name: Cup of coffee
description: The 7 g of roasted beans in one cup took about 140 liters to grow, over a thousand times the cup itself.

source.title: Chapagain & Hoekstra (2007), The water footprint of coffee and tea consumption in the Netherlands, Ecological Economics 64:109

name: Cotton T-shirt
description: One 250 g cotton T-shirt needs about 2,700 liters, what one person drinks in nearly four years.

source.title: Chapagain et al. (2006), The water footprint of cotton consumption, Ecological Economics 60:186

name: Car
description: Building one car takes 52,000 to 83,000 liters, mostly in making its steel, plastics and electronics.

source.title: Berger et al. (2012), Water footprint of European cars, Environmental Science & Technology 46:4091
source.basis: midpoint of 52,000-83,000 L for European cars

name: Chicken breast
description: Chicken needs less than a third of beef's water per kilo, but a 200 g breast still beats a bathtub.

source.title: Mekonnen & Hoekstra (2012), A global assessment of the water footprint of farm animal products, Ecosystems 15:401

name: Pork chop
description: Pigs eat a lot of grain, so a 200 g chop carries about eight full bathtubs of water.

source.title: Mekonnen & Hoekstra (2012), A global assessment of the water footprint of farm animal products, Ecosystems 15:401

name: Lamb chop
description: Sheep meat is the second thirstiest meat after beef: over 10,000 liters per kilo.

source.title: Mekonnen & Hoekstra (2012), A global assessment of the water footprint of farm animal products, Ecosystems 15:401

name: Paperback book
description: About 300 g of paper makes a paperback, needing roughly 600 liters of water.

source.title: Van Oel & Hoekstra (2012), Towards quantification of the water footprint of paper, Water Resources Management 26:733
source.basis: derived: ~10 L per 5 g A4 sheet = ~2,000 L/kg x 300 g

name: Egg
description: A single 60 g egg needs about 200 liters, almost all of it for growing the hen's feed.

source.title: Mekonnen & Hoekstra (2012), A global assessment of the water footprint of farm animal products, Ecosystems 15:401

name: Microchip
description: A tiny 2 g computer chip needs about 32 liters, largely ultra-pure water for washing wafers.

source.title: Water Footprint Network, Product Gallery

name: Bag of coffee beans
description: A 250 g bag of roasted coffee carries almost 4,750 liters, enough for 60 showers.

source.title: Mekonnen & Hoekstra (2011), The green, blue and grey water footprint of crops and derived crop products, HESS 15:1577
source.basis: 18,925 L/kg global average x 250 g; roasted coffee

name: Slice of cheese
description: It takes about 10 liters of milk to make 1 kg of cheese, so every 20 g slice hides 100 liters.

source.title: Mekonnen & Hoekstra (2012), A global assessment of the water footprint of farm animal products, Ecosystems 15:401

name: Pair of jeans
description: A pair of cotton jeans needs about 10,850 liters, mostly for irrigating the cotton.

source.title: Chapagain et al. (2006), The water footprint of cotton consumption, Ecological Economics 60:186

name: Full electric car charge
description: Charging a 60 kWh EV battery uses about 455 liters of water at US power plants.

source.title: Torcellini, Long & Judkoff (2003), Consumptive Water Use for U.S. Power Production, NREL

name: Kilogram of beef
description: The headline number of water footprints: one kilo of beef needs about 15,400 liters, enough to fill 100 bathtubs.

source.title: Mekonnen & Hoekstra (2012), A global assessment of the water footprint of farm animal products, Ecosystems 15:401

name: Bottle of water
description: A 0.5 L bottle of water takes about 1.5 liters to make, three times what's inside.

source.title: Pacific Institute (2007), Bottled Water and Energy fact sheet
source.basis: 3 L of water per 1 L bottled, incl. the bottle

name: Tablespoon of butter
description: Butter is concentrated milk fat: 5,500 liters per kilo, almost 80 liters per spoonful.

source.title: Mekonnen & Hoekstra (2012), A global assessment of the water footprint of farm animal products, Ecosystems 15:401

name: Desktop computer
description: Making a desktop PC and monitor took about 1,500 liters of water, plus 240 kg of fossil fuels.

source.title: Williams & Kuehr, eds. (2004), Computers and the Environment, United Nations University
source.basis: 24 kg desktop PC with CRT monitor

name: Slice of bread
description: A 30 g slice of wheat bread needs about 48 liters, so a whole loaf is over 1,200.

source.title: Mekonnen & Hoekstra (2011), The green, blue and grey water footprint of crops and derived crop products, HESS 15:1577

name: Cup of tea
description: Tea is five times less thirsty than coffee: about 27 liters for a 250 ml cup.

source.title: Chapagain & Hoekstra (2007), The water footprint of coffee and tea consumption in the Netherlands, Ecological Economics 64:109

name: Bowl of rice
description: A 75 g portion of rice needs about 185 liters. Paddies are among the world's thirstiest fields.

source.title: Mekonnen & Hoekstra (2011), The green, blue and grey water footprint of crops and derived crop products, HESS 15:1577
source.basis: 2,497 L/kg global average x 75 g; milled rice

name: Cotton hoodie
description: A 600 g cotton hoodie needs about 6,500 liters, more than two T-shirts' worth.

source.title: Chapagain et al. (2006), The water footprint of cotton consumption, Ecological Economics 60:186
source.basis: assumes 600 g of cotton fabric at ~10,850 L/kg

name: Plastic shopping bag
description: A 5 g plastic bag needs under a liter of water, far less than a cotton tote, though it brings other problems.

source.title: Water Footprint Calculator (GRACE), The Hidden Water in Everyday Products
source.basis: 22 gal per lb of plastic (~183 L/kg) x 5 g

name: Plate of pasta
description: 100 g of dry pasta takes about 185 liters, mostly rain falling on wheat fields.

source.title: Mekonnen & Hoekstra (2011), The green, blue and grey water footprint of crops and derived crop products, HESS 15:1577

name: Liter of gasoline
description: Refining 1 liter of gasoline consumes only 1 to 2.5 liters of water, far less than any biofuel.

source.title: Gleick (1994), Water and energy, Annual Review of Energy and the Environment 19:267
source.basis: midpoint of 1-2.5 L per L refined

name: Pizza margherita
description: A whole pizza needs about 1,260 liters: wheat, tomatoes and the cows behind the mozzarella.

source.title: Aldaya & Hoekstra (2010), The water needed for Italians to eat pasta and pizza, Agricultural Systems 103:351

name: AI chat session
description: About 30 medium-length chatbot answers need roughly a 500 ml bottle of water to cool and power the data center.

source.title: Li, Yang, Islam & Ren (2023), Making AI Less 'Thirsty': Uncovering and Addressing the Secret Water Footprint of AI Models
source.basis: GPT-3, ~16.9 ml per response (US average, on-site + off-site)

name: Bag of potato chips
description: A 200 g bag of crisps needs about 185 liters, including the oil it is fried in.

source.title: Water Footprint Network, Product Gallery

name: Glass of beer
description: A 250 ml glass of beer needs about 74 liters, mostly for the barley.

source.title: Water Footprint Network, Product Gallery

name: Kilogram of plastic
description: Making 1 kg of plastic takes about 180 liters of water.

source.title: Water Footprint Calculator (GRACE), The Hidden Water in Everyday Products

name: Bowl of popcorn
description: 30 g of popcorn kernels need about 37 liters, one of the cheapest snacks in water terms.

source.title: Mekonnen & Hoekstra (2011), The green, blue and grey water footprint of crops and derived crop products, HESS 15:1577
source.basis: 1,222 L/kg global average x 30 g; maize

name: Pair of cotton socks
description: Even a 50 g pair of cotton socks hides about 540 liters.

source.title: Chapagain et al. (2006), The water footprint of cotton consumption, Ecological Economics 60:186
source.basis: assumes 50 g of cotton fabric at ~10,850 L/kg

name: Teaspoon of sugar
description: Just 4 g of cane sugar hides about 7 liters of water.

source.title: Mekonnen & Hoekstra (2011), The green, blue and grey water footprint of crops and derived crop products, HESS 15:1577
source.basis: 1,782 L/kg global average x 4 g; refined cane sugar

name: Bowl of lentil soup
description: 60 g of dry lentils need about 350 liters. Pulses are thirsty per kilo but rich in protein.

source.title: Mekonnen & Hoekstra (2011), The green, blue and grey water footprint of crops and derived crop products, HESS 15:1577

name: 1,000 Gemini prompts
description: Google says a median Gemini prompt uses 0.26 ml of water, about five drops, so 1,000 prompts need about a quarter liter.

source.title: Google (2025), Measuring the environmental impact of delivering AI at Google scale
source.basis: 0.26 ml per median text prompt x 1,000

name: Tank of gasoline
description: A 50 L tank of gasoline takes roughly 90 liters of water to refine.

source.title: Gleick (1994), Water and energy, Annual Review of Energy and the Environment 19:267

name: Cotton tote bag
description: A 150 g cotton tote needs about 1,600 liters, so reuse it a lot.

source.title: Chapagain et al. (2006), The water footprint of cotton consumption, Ecological Economics 60:186
source.basis: assumes 150 g of cotton fabric at ~10,850 L/kg

name: Bowl of hummus
description: The 60 g of chickpeas in a bowl of hummus needed about 250 liters.

source.title: Mekonnen & Hoekstra (2011), The green, blue and grey water footprint of crops and derived crop products, HESS 15:1577

name: Glass of wine
description: A 125 ml glass of wine takes about 110 liters of water, mostly in the vineyard.

source.title: Water Footprint Network, Product Gallery

name: Soy burger
description: A 150 g soy burger needs about 160 liters, roughly 15 times less than a beef burger.

source.title: Ercin, Aldaya & Hoekstra (2012), The water footprint of soy milk and soy burger, Ecological Indicators 18:392

name: Tablespoon of olive oil
description: It takes about 5 kg of olives to make a liter of oil, so one spoon hides 200 liters.

source.title: Mekonnen & Hoekstra (2011), The green, blue and grey water footprint of crops and derived crop products, HESS 15:1577
source.basis: 14,431 L/kg global average x 14 g; virgin olive oil

name: Leather shoes
description: A pair of bovine leather shoes carries the water of the cow behind the hide.

source.title: Friends of the Earth (2015), Mind Your Step: the land and water footprints of everyday products

name: Training GPT-3
description: Training GPT-3 evaporated about 700,000 liters on site and about 5.4 million liters in total, counting the power plants.

source.title: Li, Yang, Islam & Ren (2023), Making AI Less 'Thirsty': Uncovering and Addressing the Secret Water Footprint of AI Models
source.basis: total (on-site + off-site) in US Microsoft data centers

name: Cotton ball
description: A single 0.5 g cotton ball needs about 5 liters of water.

source.title: Mekonnen & Hoekstra (2011), The green, blue and grey water footprint of crops and derived crop products, HESS 15:1577
source.basis: 9,113 L/kg global average x 0.5 g; cotton lint

name: Chocolate bar
description: A 100 g bar needs about 1,700 liters. Cocoa beans are among the thirstiest crops on earth.

source.title: Water Footprint Network, Product Gallery

name: Apple
description: A 150 g apple needs about 125 liters, mostly rain on the orchard.

source.title: Mekonnen & Hoekstra (2011), The green, blue and grey water footprint of crops and derived crop products, HESS 15:1577

name: Bottle of wine
description: A 750 ml bottle of wine carries about 650 liters, or four full bathtubs.

source.title: Water Footprint Network, Product Gallery

name: Liter of sugar beet ethanol
description: Producing 1 liter of bioethanol from sugar beet needs about 1,400 liters of water.

source.title: Gerbens-Leenes, Hoekstra & van der Meer (2009), The water footprint of bioenergy, PNAS 106:10219

name: Banana
description: A 200 g banana needs about 160 liters of water.

source.title: Mekonnen & Hoekstra (2011), The green, blue and grey water footprint of crops and derived crop products, HESS 15:1577

name: Orange
description: A 150 g orange needs about 85 liters, much less than a glass of its juice.

source.title: Mekonnen & Hoekstra (2011), The green, blue and grey water footprint of crops and derived crop products, HESS 15:1577

name: Pair of latex gloves
description: Natural rubber needs about 13,700 liters per kilo, so a 14 g pair of latex gloves hides almost 200 liters.

source.title: Mekonnen & Hoekstra (2011), The green, blue and grey water footprint of crops and derived crop products, HESS 15:1577
source.basis: 13,748 L/kg global average x 14 g; natural rubber, assumes 14 g pair

name: Hour of video streaming
description: One hour of HD streaming needs 2 to 12 liters of water at data centers and power plants.

source.title: Obringer et al. (2021), The overlooked environmental footprint of increasing Internet use, Resources, Conservation & Recycling 167:105389

name: Leather jacket
description: About 1.5 kg of leather turns a jacket into a small swimming pool of water.

source.title: Mekonnen & Hoekstra (2012), A global assessment of the water footprint of farm animal products, Ecosystems 15:401
source.basis: 17,093 L/kg global average x 1500 g; assumes ~1.5 kg of leather

name: Avocado
description: A 200 g avocado needs about 400 liters, more than three times an apple.

source.title: Mekonnen & Hoekstra (2011), The green, blue and grey water footprint of crops and derived crop products, HESS 15:1577

name: Mango
description: A 300 g mango needs about 540 liters, one of the thirstiest fruits.

source.title: Mekonnen & Hoekstra (2011), The green, blue and grey water footprint of crops and derived crop products, HESS 15:1577

name: Bottle of soda
description: A 0.5 L bottle of cola needs 150 to 300 liters, mostly hidden in its sugar.

source.title: Ercin, Aldaya & Hoekstra (2011), Corporate water footprint accounting: a sugar-containing carbonated beverage, Water Resources Management 25:721

name: Strawberry
description: One 12 g strawberry needs only about 4 liters, one of the thriftiest fruits.

source.title: Mekonnen & Hoekstra (2011), The green, blue and grey water footprint of crops and derived crop products, HESS 15:1577

name: Rose
description: A single cut rose from Kenya needs 7 to 13 liters of water.

source.title: Mekonnen, Hoekstra & Becht (2012), Mitigating the water footprint of export cut flowers from the Lake Naivasha Basin, Kenya, Water Resources Management 26:3725

name: Liter of soybean biodiesel
description: One liter of biodiesel from soybeans needs about 14,000 liters of water.

source.title: Gerbens-Leenes, Hoekstra & van der Meer (2009), The water footprint of bioenergy, PNAS 106:10219

name: Cherry
description: A single 8 g cherry needs about 13 liters, about three times a strawberry.

source.title: Mekonnen & Hoekstra (2011), The green, blue and grey water footprint of crops and derived crop products, HESS 15:1577

name: Hour-long video call
description: An hour of video calls needs 2 to 12 liters. Turning the camera off cuts that by about 96%.

source.title: Obringer et al. (2021), The overlooked environmental footprint of increasing Internet use, Resources, Conservation & Recycling 167:105389

name: Kiwi
description: A 75 g kiwi needs about 39 liters of water.

source.title: Mekonnen & Hoekstra (2011), The green, blue and grey water footprint of crops and derived crop products, HESS 15:1577

name: Leather wallet
description: Bovine leather is one of the thirstiest materials: 17,000 liters per kilo of hide.

source.title: Mekonnen & Hoekstra (2012), A global assessment of the water footprint of farm animal products, Ecosystems 15:401
source.basis: 17,093 L/kg global average x 100 g; assumes ~100 g of leather

name: Pineapple
description: A whole 1 kg pineapple needs only about 255 liters, a bargain per bite.

source.title: Mekonnen & Hoekstra (2011), The green, blue and grey water footprint of crops and derived crop products, HESS 15:1577

name: Cigarette
description: The 0.7 g of tobacco in one cigarette needs about 2 liters of water.

source.title: Mekonnen & Hoekstra (2011), The green, blue and grey water footprint of crops and derived crop products, HESS 15:1577
source.basis: 2,925 L/kg global average x 0.7 g; unmanufactured tobacco

name: Glass of orange juice
description: Squeezing a 200 ml glass takes several oranges, and about 200 liters of water.

description: A 5 kg watermelon needs about 1,200 liters, but it is over 90% water itself.

source.title: Mekonnen & Hoekstra (2011), The green, blue and grey water footprint of crops and derived crop products, HESS 15:1577

name: Bitcoin transaction
description: A single Bitcoin transaction uses about 16,000 liters, enough to fill a backyard pool.

source.title: de Vries (2023), Bitcoin's growing water footprint, Cell Reports Sustainability

name: Date
description: A single 8 g date needs about 18 liters, grown in the desert.

source.title: Mekonnen & Hoekstra (2011), The green, blue and grey water footprint of crops and derived crop products, HESS 15:1577

name: Liter of jatropha biodiesel
description: Jatropha biodiesel was sold as a drought-proof fuel, yet each liter needs about 20,000 liters of water.

source.title: Gerbens-Leenes, Hoekstra & van der Meer (2009), The water footprint of bioenergy, PNAS 106:10219

name: Coconut
description: A coconut (about 700 g of nut) needs nearly 1,900 liters of water.

source.title: Mekonnen & Hoekstra (2011), The green, blue and grey water footprint of crops and derived crop products, HESS 15:1577

name: Leather belt
